article_sentences: Amaravati: Cyclone Arnab has devastated Andhra Pradesh’s coastal districts, turning harvest-ready fields into waterlogged expanses, destroying plantations and leaving fishing families facing the loss of their livelihoods.
In the Godavari region, violent winds and torrential rain flattened paddy crops just weeks before harvest, while towering sea waves damaged coastal settlements and smashed nearly 450 fishing boats.
Flooding rivers have isolated villages, disrupted highways and railway services, and intensified hardships for thousands of families.
The cyclone struck the undivided East Godavari region around midnight on Tuesday, with winds reaching 100–120 kmph.
Along the Kakinada and Konaseema coasts, the sea reportedly advanced up to 500 metres inland, damaging homes, roads and protective sea walls.
Nearly 450 boats, each valued between Rs 5 lakh and Rs 50 lakh, were damaged or destroyed.
Many fishermen had bought them with borrowed money, leaving families without their principal source of income and burdened with debt.
Konaseema suffered extensive agricultural damage, with more than one lakh acres- and estimates reaching 1.16 lakh acres- of paddy submerged.
Banana and coconut plantations were devastated in Enugula Mahal, Vanapalli and other areas.
Horticultural crops across an estimated 12,000 acres were damaged.
Rajamahendravaram constituency reported losses across more than 25,000 acres, while East Godavari and Kakinada districts reported crop damage across approximately 50,000 hectares each.
In Anakapalli, more than 7,000 hectares of crops were submerged.

stories.title: Andhra Pradesh Minister tells official to expedite restoration works in cyclone-hit towns

article_sentences: Municipal Administration and Urban Development Minister P. Narayana on Thursday directed the officials to expedite restoration works and bring life back to normal in cyclone-affected areas across Andhra Pradesh.

During a teleconference with Municipal Administration Department Commissioner and Director P. Sampath Kumar, Public Health Engineering-in-Chief Prabhakar and Municipal Commissioners, the Minister reviewed the damage caused by Cyclone Arnab and the progress of relief and restoration measures.
Officials informed the Minister that 85 locations in 10 municipalities across eight districts had been affected by the cyclone.
Normalcy had been restored in 71 locations across seven municipalities so far, they said.
The officials said that fallen trees and electric poles had been cleared.
In areas where power supply remained disrupted, drinking water was being supplied using generators to ensure that residents did not face shortages.
Mr. Narayana instructed the Municipal Commissioners to prioritise sanitation and maintain cleanliness in affected localities to prevent public health problems.
He directed officials to ensure that streetlights were fully functional by Thursday evening.
The Minister stressed the need for coordinated efforts among departments to complete the restoration works swiftly.

stories.title: Post-Arnab cyclone, heavy rain wreaks havoc in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati districts

article_sentences: Heavy rain triggered by cyclone Arnab wreaked havoc in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal districts on Thursday (October 29, 2026), washing away roads, marooning villages and triggering landslides, as State officials struggled to restore normalcy.
The rainfall recorded in the three districts was among the highest ever recorded.
“Exceptionally heavy rainfall occurred over south Odisha during the past 24 hours, ending at 8.30 a.m. on Thursday.

The highest rainfall of 546 mm was recorded at Patrapur [Ganjam], followed by 503 mm at Sorada [Ganjam], 462 mm at G. Udayagiri [Kandhamal], 458 mm at Mahendragarh [Gajapati], 388 mm at Sanakhemundi [Ganjam] and 309 mm at Chikiti (Ganjam),” the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
A stretch of the National Highway 326 connecting Berhampur with Mohana was washed away by swirling floodwaters, disrupting road connectivity.
Road infrastructure also suffered extensive damage in Gajapati district.
The hilly terrain compounded the situation, as torrents of rainwater rushed downhill into low-lying areas, triggering landslides and damaging infrastructure.
At several places, floodwaters flowed over major roads, halting vehicular movement in the two districts.
In Ganjam district alone, 42,500 people were marooned by floodwaters, while 11,000 people were shifted from vulnerable areas to designated shelters.
With roads cut off and hundreds of villages inundated by floodwaters in Ganjam, the State government roped in the Coast Guard to airlift people stranded in Dharakote block.

“In response to a distress call received from the Ganjam district administration on the morning of October 29, 2026, the Coast Guard Air Enclave, Bhubaneswar, scrambled an ALH Mk-III helicopter despite severe weather conditions,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.
“Despite challenging conditions, the aircrew located the heavily inundated Public Health Centre in Jagmohan, where people were stranded by floodwaters following the storm.

stories.headline: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
stories.title: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
stories.summary: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A reported glacial lake outburst in Bhutan prompted evacuation warnings downstream in West Bengal.
Authorities are assessing the discharge while monitoring the Sankosh River for a possible surge.
A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) has been reported at Shintaphu Lake in Bhutan, raising concerns over a sudden surge of water flowing downstream into India.
The Government of India has issued a special advisory for parts of West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels could rise sharply along the Sankosh River.
The outburst was reported on Thursday evening at Shintaphu Lake, located below Wakila Mountain in Lungo, Laya Gewog, in Bhutan's Gasa district.
Sirens were sounded to alert people living near riverbanks, while residents in the affected area were reportedly moved to safer ground.
Shintaphu Lake is among Bhutan's 17 potentially dangerous glacial lakes.

An official from the National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) said a water-level monitoring station was located at Taktsimakhang, but no alert had been triggered there at the time of the initial reports.
The extent of the outburst and its downstream impact remained unclear.
A GLOF occurs when water stored in a lake formed by melting glaciers is suddenly released, often after a natural barrier fails or is breached.
The resulting surge can travel rapidly through mountain valleys, carrying debris and damaging settlements, roads, bridges and farmland.
Shintaphu Lake lies within Bhutan's Punatsangchhu river basin.

stories.headline: Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme
stories.title: Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme
stories.summary: On October 28, the Union Cabinet approved the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme with an outlay of INR 1,856.67 crore. The money will be spent from 2027 to 2034. This scheme was first announced in the Union Budget along with a timeline that matters, as often we have seen good ideas often stay on paper only. Currently, India produces a lot of sports goods. A case in point is Jalandhar and Meerut. The two big centres are popular for making sports items and products. Together the two cities have over 250 exporting units and nearly 20,000 household units. About 90% of production comes from small and micro firms. Especially the bat manufacturing industry is massive, India producers are experts in the field. Indian brands and makers hold about 75% to 80% of the global cricket bat market. But our equipment exports are only $275 million. The world exports about $52 billion. That gap is massive. Smaller firms find it hard to expand. As per the provision of this scheme they lack testing labs, design help and obviously financial assistance. They also struggle to get the certificates that foreign buyers ask for. How will the scheme work? The scheme will probably work on multiple fronts (six-stages). On the first level, it plans manufacturing zones. These will bring makers, suppliers, testing labs and design centres to one place. There may be four such zones, each over 300 acres. While on the second stage it offers money for investment. Anchor investors who put in at least INR 100 crore get 20% support on capital spending. Makers who invest INR 10 crore or more can get up to 15% as turnover-linked support. Together, these two parts have INR 1,130 crore. In the third stage, it helps in holding up existing clusters that are already on the ground. Shared facilities will be upgraded, with costs split with the States. This is where small firms stand to gain most. In the fourth stage, it pays for certification. INR 105 crore is set aside. The government will cover 70% of the cost of a first certificate and 50% of renewals. A bat or a helmet with an international seal sells more easily abroad. It backs new ideas on the fifth vertical. Centres of Excellence will study materials and protective gear. Start-ups registered with DPIIT can get grants of up to INR 20 lakh. On the sixth level, which is the outreach stage, it covers skills and marketing. There will be training, an India Sports Expo and a Brand India campaign. Relying on other schemes Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme will take assistance from other schemes. For instance the zones will use land and sheds from the BHAVYA scheme and NICDC industrial parks. Research will link with the Anusandhan National Research Foundation. Marketing will use the Export Promotion Mission. This is termed to be a very sensible and useful measure. The government is not building everything new. It is patching the gaps from the already existing design. The design will not only give cash to the beneficiaries but will fix the whole chain, from factory to certificate to buyer. However, there remains some pertinent questions. For example, large investors will gain from the 20% support. Will small firms see the same benefit? Nearly 90% of the sector is small, so the scheme must reach them. The cluster upgrades will decide that. Land acquisition will be another test to determine the positive outcome. Zones of 300 acres need clearances and State cooperation. If there are any delays there it means it will slow down everything. Besides, what matters more is the timing. As we know Los Angeles will be hosting the Olympics in 2028. Ahmedabad is also going to host the Commonwealth Games in 2030. Brisbane follows in 2032. So there is every possibility that the demand for equipment will rise in the coming years. What authorities are trying to gain out of this scheme, is that it wants India to make more of its own sports goods and import less. It wants more exports, more jobs and better quality. As per the official estimation predictions, the exports could reach $8.1 billion by 2036 which implies as many as 54 lakh jobs. That is a big leap if executed well. Furthermore, this scheme has been made to develop a strong relationship between sport and industry. As Khelo India builds players. This scheme is going to build the equipment they use. If both work, an Indian athlete may one day train, and win, with gear made in Jalandhar or Meerut. That is the ultimate goal of Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme. (COURTESY: PIB SRINAGAR)

stories.summary: Kashmir is facing a crisis as its snowfall declines. This reduction affects not just the landscape but also the people and the environment. Recent studies show a strong link between decreasing snowfall in Kashmir and global warming. As the region experiences unusual winter weather, experts warn that the effects go beyond just beautiful scenery. This trend highlights the urgent need for global climate action. For generations, Chillai Kalan, a harsh 40-day winter, shaped life in the Kashmir Valley. It usually brought a thick layer of snow that acted as a natural reservoir, protecting the region's delicate ecosystem. Recent winters look very different. Snowfall is decreasing and arriving later, so it can't properly fill the glaciers or recharge groundwater. This change affects more than just Kashmir's famous winter beauty; it highlights a growing climate crisis. With less snow, the valley faces serious risks to its water supply and farming economy. Fewer snowflakes mean less water for rivers and crops. Recent studies indicate that snowfall has declined by more than 30% over the past two decades, raising alarm among environmental scientists and residents alike. With snow serving as a vital water source for agriculture and hydropower, the implications of this shift are profound and far-reaching. Local farmers are reporting lower crop yields, worsening food shortages in a region already facing high unemployment and limited resources. As temperatures rise and snowfall decreases, habitats face serious stress, which could lead to extinctions and ecosystem changes. The tourism-based economy of Kashmir, which relies on winter sports and beautiful scenery, is also at risk, threatening jobs and local businesses. Why Kashmir's Flood Red Flags Went Unheard Kashmir’s floods are usually called natural disasters. However, the reality is more troubling: the floods have become administrative failures caused by neglect and poor policies. Years ago, engineers and experts warned that Srinagar was heading for a flood disaster. Er. Ghulam Nabi Mirti wrote an important article called “Fighting Floods Fury in Kashmir” on September 29, 2006, in the local newspaper. He detailed how illegal constructions, silt buildup in the River Jhelum, shrinking wetlands, and uncontrolled urban growth were putting Srinagar at risk. The article highlighted vulnerable areas such as Lasjan, Padshahibagh, Soiteng, Nowgam, Rakhi Shalina, and Mehjoor Nagar. These places faced huge losses during the 2014 floods. The warnings were based on science and technical data. However, those in charge overlooked this warning, and, sadly, similar disasters have continued to occur since the 2014 floods The policymakers need to research and examine: Scientific dredging of the River Jhelum. Restoration of flood spill channels. Protection of wetlands. Elimination of encroachments. Reinforcement of bunds. Advanced flood forecasting systems. Kashmir’s Farmlands Are Disappearing Fast: What Can Be Done? In the last thirty years, Kashmir has changed quickly. Buildings are replacing fertile rice fields and orchards. The landscape that was once focused on farming now includes shopping centers, homes, roads, and schools. This fast loss of farmland affects food security, jobs, the environment, and the way Kashmiris live. Villages near Srinagar, Budgam, Pulwama, Baramulla, Anantnag, and Ganderbal are heavily affected. Some studies show that since the early 2000s, thousands of hectares of farmland have been converted to non-agricultural uses. In today's climate, strong agriculture is vital to regional strength. Constant land development weakens the Valley’s ability to adapt and makes both city and countryside residents more at risk during extreme weather. The environmental issues in Kashmir On August 14, 2025, Kishtwar in the Chenab Valley suffered a severe cloudburst. More than 67 people died, nearly 200 went missing, and 300 were injured. Another incident happened in the Kathua region. Why are cloudbursts happening so frequently, and what can we do about it? The Kashmir Himalayas are a fertile ground for cloudbursts. This happens because two weather systems affect the area. We get moisture from western disturbances and the southwest monsoon, which brings moisture from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. When moisture reaches Kashmir, it gathers in heavy clouds. Strong winds quickly push this moisture up, reaching the Himalayas and forming dense clouds. After a while, these clouds become too heavy for the atmosphere to hold. When they can't support the weight anymore, they burst. This is called a cloudburst. It has recently happened in Kishtwar, Kathua, and Uttarakhand. We have stripped away all the trees in the forest. We are building big concrete structures, mining, cutting down trees, and changing the use of the land. This loose soil mixes with heavy rain, causing flash floods. These floods destroy everything in their path, including lives, buildings, and more. The study shows that the world is already feeling the effects of a warming planet. In Kashmir, this results in unpredictable rainfall. The area is changing from steady snowfall to sudden heavy rain, which the land cannot handle. This significantly increases the risk of severe flash floods and landslides, such as the disastrous floods that hit the valley in 2014. The region is getting warmer. In July 2024, Kashmir experienced an unusual heatwave, with record-high temperatures. This shows a shift towards subtropical heat in an area that usually has a temperate climate. Extreme weather events are increasing in number and severity. From 2010 to 2022, the region experienced over 2,800 such events, including heavy rains, flash floods, cloudbursts, and landslides, which caused major loss of life and property. What Has The Paris Agreement Achieved After 11 Years Of Action? More than a decade after the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, the global approach to climate change has changed. However, it still struggles to meet its main objectives. Eleven years after the important meeting in Paris, the results of the Paris Agreement are mixed. The agreement has helped prevent a harmful rise in temperatures, but it has also highlighted major political divides. This March, temperatures in Kashmir are hitting record highs usually seen in May. This unusual heat raises worries about climate change and its effects in the area, known for its beautiful winter scenery. As we reflect on a decade of commitments, we see a sad irony: the countries that contributed the least to climate change are suffering the most. These nations often bear the burden, paying for the emissions of wealthier countries through their own hardship and debt. (The Author is a Bio Consultant and can be reached at: ask@tahirmaqsood.com )

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 29, 2026) declared unconstitutional a Karnataka State law, which validated the 2011 selection of Gazetted Probationers made through what the court described as a “corrupt” and “blatantly nepotistic” recruitment process conducted by the State Public Service Commission.

A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran held that the Karnataka Civil Services (Validation of Selection and Appointment of 2011 Batch Gazetted Probationers) Act, 2022, was enacted clearly with the intent to countermand the judgments of both the Karnataka High Court and the Supreme Court.
The courts had upheld the decision to cancel the entire 2011 recruitment process for 362 posts of Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ Officers.

“The cancellation having been upheld by the High Court and the Supreme Court, the power does not lie with the legislature to annul the cancellation, even by a legislation, and thus nullify the judgments of the Constitutional courts,” Justice Chandran said.
The court highlighted how the State government, represented by senior advocate Kapil Sibal, constantly changed its position over a decade “depending on the hues and colours in the changing times”.

The State had, over the years, swung between supporting the cancellation of the entire recruitment process and enacting the 2022 law, leaving the hapless candidates caught in the crosshairs of shifting political whims and systemic failure.

“When the winds of politics change direction, it is the common man who gets caught in the storm… A recruitment of 2011 is hanging fire still, putting to peril the aspirations of many… Six appellants [represented by senior advocate Shyam Divan] who would be over-aged now have relentlessly pursued their cause in their zeal to join the Karnataka Civil Services,” Justice Chandran observed.
The 2011 recruitment process saw 1,38,307 people apply.

Two years later, a Criminal Investigation Department (CID) inquiry found “gross manipulations” in the process, and “the irregularities in evaluation of answer scripts were found to be shockingly disgraceful”.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court upheld the cancellation of the entire recruitment based on a 2011 notification.
It said no equity could be granted to untainted successful candidates, represented by senior advocate Sanjay Nuli, who were selected on the strength of the 2022 Act.
The court termed the Act a “stillborn legislation”.

A Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale said the right to religious freedom was also subject to public health and the protection of fundamental rights.

article_sentences: Observing that banks must be made accountable to indemnify losses of victims of digital fraud, the Supreme Court on Thursday (October 29, 2026) said victims of offences like digital arrests should receive compensation of at least the amount lost if the fraud is found to have resulted from a failure of due diligence by the financial institution.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said it would examine the Reserve Bank of India's proposed Know Your Customer (KYC) Amendment Directions, 2026, which are expected to be notified by November 30 and operationalised by December 31.
The Bench stressed that the proposed regulatory framework must provide for suitable compensation to victims where financial institutions are found to have failed in their due diligence obligations.

It also reiterated the need for mandatory preventive measures, including temporarily suspending unusual transactions that deviate from an account holder's established transaction pattern, automated reporting of suspicious activity and physical verification to establish the genuineness of transactions.
The Court further said that it is the responsibility of banks to alert neighbouring police stations about unusual transactions involving customers who may be victims of digital arrest scams.
The Bench asked the RBI to provide details of the financial institutions that would be covered by the proposed guidelines and the measures being considered to compensate victims for their losses.

During the hearing, Attorney General R. Venkataramani, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, informed the Court that reported digital arrest cases had declined by around 50% compared with the previous year, attributing the reduction to the Court's intervention, coordinated action by government ministries and departments, and public awareness campaigns.
The CJI, however, pointed out that the country had still suffered losses of nearly ₹800 crore from such offences this year.

The CJI identified two key areas requiring further intervention, the accountability of banks and the problem of mule accounts, which are frequently used to receive and transfer proceeds of cybercrime.

The matter, titled In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest Related to Forged Documents, is being monitored by the Supreme Court as part of efforts to strengthen the country's institutional response to cyber-enabled financial fraud.

stories.headline: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.title: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.summary: Livestock and agriculture production is considered as the backbone of India’s economy and food security. Despite rapid industrialization, over 46% of India’s total workforce is engaged in agriculture and allied sectors, while roughly 60-65% of the population depends on it for their primary livelihood. However, these sectors have undergone an intense transformation since independence of India in 1947. Indian agriculture during pre- independence was characterized by traditional farming practices like using of tillers, sickles and manual labour with little or no mechanization which eventually resulted in low productivity. Livestock has traditionally complemented crop cultivation by providing a source of draught power, manure, milk and hence an additional household income. It also provided financial security to the families during periods of economic distress. Immediately after independence, India faced widespread poverty, low agricultural productivity and an urgent need to strengthen India’s economy. Following independence, agricultural research, irrigation facilities, improved seeds, fertilization and mechanization gradually transformed agricultural and livestock production. Over time, these initiatives contributed to major agricultural transformations commonly described as Green, White, Blue and Golden Revolutions. The history of livestock and agricultural development cannot be understood only through the increase in production. An introspective assessment must also examine who benefited from these developments, what environmental burdens accompanied them and whether leads to lasting prosperity for farmers and other livestock owners. Livestock and Agriculture during the Pre-independence Era Livestock formed an essential component of traditional farming system. Cattle and buffaloes served draught power while manure was used as a fertilizer for soil. Milk and its byproducts served as a household nutrition and also provided income. Indigenous breeds had valuable adaptive characteristics like tolerance to local climatic conditions and ability to survive under low input management systems. But, livestock productivity was restricted by insufficient nutrition, infectious diseases and parasitic infections. Treatment of animals in many rural areas depended on traditional knowledge and locally available traditional remedies and access to veterinary hospitals was limited. Dairy marketing was also unorganized and inadequate milk collection, chilling, processing and transportation facilities limited the commercial potential of livestock production. Limited availability of scientific support and organized infrastructure further restricted their capacity to improve production. During the pre-independence era, Indian agriculture was predominantly dependent on rainfall, local seeds and manual labour. Farming was primarily meeting the household food requirements and there was a limited access to modern agricultural machinery, irrigation and other scientific facilities. Due to inadequate irrigation, limited availability of good quality seeds and insufficient fertilizers, agricultural productivity was also low. Farmers were prone to droughts, floods and other natural calamities. Poor storage and transportation facilities further restricted the movement of agricultural production and increased post-harvest losses. Colonial land revenue system further contributed to unequal relationships between land-owners and cultivators. This practice often limited farmers’ ability to invest in irrigation, soil improvement and other long-term agricultural assets which ultimately lead to crop failure, disease outbreaks and other economic losses. Before the widespread expansion of monetized rural markets, barter and customary exchange arrangements played important roles in various village economies. Livestock and agricultural produce was exchanged for essential items and household goods. Sometimes, occupational groups used to receive a share of the produce and harvest in return for their services. These arrangements strengthened interdependence within rural communities but it also restricted economic exchange only to local networks and limit farmers’ bargaining power and accumulate savings. As commercial agriculture expanded, monetary transactions and regulated markets gradually became more important. Farmers gained more opportunities to sell their produce for money and purchase essential inputs like seeds, fertilizers, machinery etc. But this transition didn’t ensure fair returns to primary producers due to transportation cost, price fluctuation and inadequate storage. The historical transition from barter to organized agricultural marketing indicates an important economic change but it also reflects the need for transparent markets and profitable prices. Post-Independence Transformation: Revolution in Agriculture and Allied Sciences After independence, land reforms became an important element of India’s rural development strategy. The abolition of intermediary landholding systems, tenancy reforms and redistribution of surplus land were intended to minimize exploitation and the condition of cultivators. The principle of land to the tiller represented the idea that those who cultivate the land should enjoy greater security and receive a fairer share of benefits produced by their labour. However, its application varied from state to state. Incomplete land records, resistance from powerful landowners meant that landlessness and unequal access to productive resources persisted. Land fragmentation was the other major challenge. Population growth and subsequent division of agricultural holdings among generations contributed to smaller and more scattered landholdings. These conditions limited the use of machinery, irrigation investments, crop diversification and the economic viability of farming. The Green revolution, which was introduced during the mid-1960s, marked a significant transformation in Indian agriculture. Dr. M. S. Swaminathan played a pivotal role in India’s Green Revolution, while Dr. Norman Borlaug made internationally recognised contributions to the development and dissemination of high-yielding wheat varieties. From severe food deficiency and low crop productivity to self-sufficient agricultural production by adopting high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice alongside irrigation, chemical fertilizers and improved agricultural machinery, agricultural research, improved seeds and extension services further contributed to increase in food-grain production. These developments strengthened national food security and decreased India’s susceptibility to food shortages. However, these gains were geographically uneven with irrigated regions generally benefitting more than rain fed areas. The environmental exploitation also became evident with intensive cultivation and excessive groundwater extraction. The extensive usage of fertilizers and pesticides further contributed to the soil degradation, water pollution and ecological disturbances. The White Revolution transformed India’s dairy sector through organized milk production, institutional cooperation, improved breeding programs, better animal nutrition and veterinary support. An important foundation of this transformation was the establishment of the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union at Anand, Gujarat, in 1946, which later became closely associated with the Amul brand. The cooperative model enabled milk producers to collectively market their produce and obtain a more organised connection with consumers. Dr. Verghese Kurien, widely recognised as the Father of India’s White Revolution, played a central role in expanding this cooperative model. The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB), established in 1965, subsequently promoted the Anand Pattern of dairy cooperatives across the country through Operation Flood, launched in 1970. Operation Flood was implemented in phases and helped strengthen India’s dairy infrastructure, organised milk procurement and rural dairy economy. This revolution enhanced the importance of livestock as an economic asset rather than merely a source of draught power. Due to this, cattle and buffaloes became important contributors to household income. The expansion of dairying exposed persistent challenges also. Inadequate green fodder, high feed costs, reproductive disorders, mastitis and heat stress decreased the productivity and hence profitability. Moreover indiscriminate crossbreeding without taking attention to nutrition and healthcare compromised animal welfare. The Blue Revolution focused on development of fisheries and aquaculture to provide nutritional security and improve rural income. Post-independence investments in aquaculture helped in strengthening the fisheries sector and offer important opportunities for rural employment, entrepreneurship and affordable animal protein. However, the expansion of fisheries created environmental concerns like water pollution, eutrophication, habitat destruction, disease outbreaks in intensive aquaculture and salanisation of agricultural land. The Golden revolution between 1991 and 2003 refers to the rapid rise of India’s horticulture sector including fruits, vegetables, flowers and other high value crops. Improved planting material, irrigation, scientific grading and transportation created opportunities for farmers to generate higher returns per unit of land. Horticulture farmers face peculiar economic risks. Perishable produce must be sold within a limited time period, making farmers susceptible when transportation or storage facilities are inadequate. Sudden price drop during peak harvest season eventually reduce farm income. Modernization of livestock and agriculture production Beyond the major agricultural revolutions, the post-independence period witnessed considerable changes in farm inputs, machinery, animal breeding and livestock management. High yielding seeds, chemical fertilizers, tractors, threshers, harvesters and irrigation equipment increased the production and reduced the time required for many farming operations. Rural roads and the expansion of agricultural markets improved connectivity between producers and consumers. At the time of independence in 1947, India did not have dedicated agricultural universities but only 17 agricultural or veterinary colleges affiliated with general universities. Today, India has approximately 74 agricultural and allied universities recognized by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR).The ICAR Lab-to-Land Programme, launched in 1979, was specifically designed to transfer viable technologies from laboratories to farmers’ fields. Krishi Vigyan Kendras and other extension initiatives further strengthen the connection between scientific research and practical farming. However, rising input costs, excessive fertiliser use, pesticide residues, machinery related expenses and the exclusion of resource-poor farmers from technology-intensive systems remain important concerns. Industrialisation and urbanisation create additional pressures through pollution, waste generation and the conversion of agricultural land into non-agricultural uses. Road connectivity has also influenced agricultural development. Improved roads facilitate the movement of farm produces, veterinary supplies and other essential services. But farmers in many remote areas experienced high transportation costs, inadequate storage facilities and limited processing opportunities. Better connectivity must therefore be complemented by transparent marketing, reliable procurement, storage facility and opportunities for value addition. Currently, India possesses one of the world’s largest livestock populations and is also the world’s largest milk producer, reflecting the importance of livestock in its agricultural economy. Livestock development benefited from genetic improvement, artificial insemination, improved nutrition, vaccination, disease diagnosis and reproductive management. Crossbreeding of indigenous cattle with exotic dairy breeds contributed to increased milk production in many production systems. Improved management of indigenous breeds and the conservation of locally adapted genetic resources also became increasingly important. Timely diagnosis of diseases, access to qualified veterinary professionals and responsible use of medicines remain essential for sustainable livestock development. In livestock sector also, the benefits didn’t reach all livestock owners equally and there was also shortage of veterinary services, inadequate fodder and insufficient infrastructure. Poor manure management can contribute to water contamination and inadequate waste disposal and unsuitable housing can affect animal health. Climate change presents an additional challenge to livestock production by affecting temperature patterns, rainfall distribution, water availability, fodder production and the condition of grazing and pasture lands. Livestock may consequently face changing risks from emerging, re-emerging and endemic infectious diseases. Changes in disease ecology can also complicate surveillance and control, while the evolution and spread of pathogens may increase the challenges faced by veterinary health systems. Future directions for Sustainable Livestock and Agricultural development India’s next phase of agricultural development must focus on farmer prosperity, efficient resource use and resilience rather than production alone. The following priorities deserve attention: Sustainable crop production by promoting soil testing, balanced fertilisation, improved seed quality and climate resilient farming practices. Efficient water management by encouraging rainwater harvesting, groundwater monitoring and cropping patterns compatible with local water availability. Improved market infrastructure by strengthening rural roads, storage and processing facilities and transparent marketing. Affordable veterinary healthcare by expanding veterinary services, timely disease diagnosis and access to qualified veterinary professionals. Integrated livestock management by improving fodder availability, balanced rations, reproductive management, hygienic milk production and prevention of economically important diseases. Responsible breeding programmes by combining improved genes with adaptability, fertility, disease resistance and animal welfare. Environmental protection by reducing pollution, encouraging manure management and efficient and judicious use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides, veterinary drugs and water resources. Conclusion The transition in scenario of livestock and agriculture from pre-independence era to post-independence era of India represents a major transformation in livestock and agricultural production. Traditional farming system based on animal power, local resources and barter system has been supplemented by scientific crop production, mechanisation, organised markets, and improved livestock breeding and modern veterinary healthcare. The Green Revolution strengthened food security, White Revolution transformed dairy sector, Blue Revolution improved fisheries sector and Golden Revolution increased the horticulture production. However, increased production has not eliminated land fragmentation, livestock related financial pressures or environmental degradation. Farmers continue to face challenges with fluctuating prices, natural calamities and limited infrastructure. The future of Indian livestock and agriculture industry depends on balancing productivity with profitability, environmental responsibility, economic security of farmers and long-term resilience of rural communities. ( The Author is HOD Veterinary Medicine, SKUAST Kashmir)

stories.headline: J&K faces Rs 95 lakh interest bill for delayed power payments
stories.title: J&K faces Rs 95 lakh interest bill for delayed power payments
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 29: Jammu and Kashmir has been saddled with an interest liability of nearly Rs 95 lakh for delays in clearing electricity-related payments, an amount that has added to the financial burden of its power sector without bringing any additional electricity to consumers. The liability, disclosed in a fresh statement issued by the Northern Regional Power Committee (NRPC), is the highest among 140 utilities and entities listed across northern India and accounts for nearly 45 per cent of the region's total interest payable for the April-June quarter of 2026. The figures come as Kashmir heads into winter, when electricity demand rises and the power department faces the annual challenge of maintaining supply to households and businesses. According to a Document by NRPC, dated October 27, accessed by Rising Kashmir, Jammu and Kashmir has been assessed Rs 94,95,917.56 as interest on delayed payment of deviation settlement charges. The total interest payable by all listed utilities stands at Rs 2.12 crore. Punjab has been assessed just Rs 26,021, while Delhi, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand have no interest payable against their names. Jammu and Kashmir's interest liability is more than 365 times that of Punjab. The charges arise from a mechanism through which power utilities settle differences between the electricity they were scheduled to draw from the grid and what they actually drew. Payments under this mechanism must be cleared within prescribed timelines, with delays attracting interest. For Jammu and Kashmir, the Rs 95 lakh is therefore not a payment towards purchasing electricity. It is an additional financial obligation arising because payments were delayed. While the interest liability cannot be directly linked to any particular power cut or increase in consumer tariffs, it represents an expense that could have been avoided through timely settlement of dues. The NRPC statement does not explain why Jammu and Kashmir accumulated such a large interest amount or identify the individual payments responsible for it. It also does not disclose the principal amount involved or whether the interest has since been cleared. The figures have emerged against the backdrop of continuing concerns over Jammu and Kashmir's ability to meet electricity demand during the colder months, particularly in the Valley, where dependence on electricity for heating places additional pressure on the system. The financial position of the power sector assumes added importance during this period, when arrangements for electricity procurement and grid management become crucial to maintaining supplies. The NRPC has given utilities 15 days from October 27 to point out any discrepancies in the calculations. In the absence of objections, the amounts will be treated as final. The committee has asked the concerned entities to deposit the interest into the Northern Region Deviation Pool Account maintained by the Northern Regional Load Despatch Centre. The statement covers the first quarter of 2026-27 alone, leaving open the question of whether further interest liabilities have accumulated since June.
